clue.text: A revolutionary leader '. memorised some slang

indicators.note: the leader of the word revolutionary is its opening letter, the one at the front

parts.note: to have got something is to have learnt it by heart, memorised it

explanation.surface: A rebel chief has learnt by heart some street slang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary leader' looks like a phrase for Lenin or Castro, but 'leader' just asks for the first letter of 'revolutionary'.
explanation.definitionFit: Argot is the private jargon or cant of a group, a kind of slang.

clue.text: Broken rails and bats used as weapons at one time

indicators.note: broken means smashed apart, so the letters are reassembled

explanation.surface: Smashed railings and cricket bats were once used as weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broken' mixes the letters of 'rails' and 'bats'; 'and' joins the two words of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossbows of the medieval period, the plural of arbalest, were weapons long ago.

clue.text: The appearance of sound men

indicators.note: sound means as heard, so the word for men is said and its sound spelt another way

parts.note: guys is informal for men

explanation.surface: The look of healthy, robust men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like an adjective meaning healthy, but it says that the word for men is heard.
explanation.definitionFit: A guise is an outward appearance or semblance, often a false one.

clue.text: Underclothing stuffed into a carrier — it could occasion ridicule

indicators.note: stuffed into means pushed inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a tray carries plates and cups
a vest is an undershirt in British English

explanation.surface: Underwear crammed into a basket could make someone a laughing stock.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a vest is an undergarment worn under a shirt, not a waistcoat.
explanation.definitionFit: A grotesque parody or absurd misrepresentation invites mockery.

clue.text: Scattered and disappeared — about time!

indicators.note: about means going round, so one word is placed around the other

parts.note: died, as in a fire or a sound that died, means disappeared
a spell is a period of time

explanation.surface: Someone exasperated: the crowd scattered and vanished, and about time too!
explanation.walkthrough: 'about time!' reads as an exclamation of relief, but 'about' puts DIED round SPELL.
explanation.definitionFit: To dispel is to drive away or disperse, so a dispelled crowd has been scattered.

clue.text: Many an individual finds this, socially acceptable'

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for five hundred, a large number
one is a single individual

explanation.surface: Many a person thinks this the proper way to behave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Many' stands for a large Roman numeral, D (500); 'finds this' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: The proper or approved thing to do, as in 'it isn't the thing to do', is correct etiquette.

clue.text: Place on Oriental railway providing material for a writer

indicators.note: on, in a down clue, sets the first piece above the others

parts.note: a station is a place or post, as in a station in life
E stands for East, the Orient

explanation.surface: A post on an Eastern railway supplies a writer's needs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oriental' gives E for East, and RY abbreviates railway; 'providing' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing paper, envelopes and pens are the supplies a correspondent uses.

clue.text: A quarter bloom in spring

parts.note: E for East is one of the four quarters of the compass
an aster is a daisy-like flower

explanation.surface: A fourth of the flowers come out in springtime.
explanation.walkthrough: The four compass points are often called quarters, so 'A quarter' is E for East.
explanation.definitionFit: The Christian festival of the Resurrection falls in spring each year.

clue.text: Insubstantial craft that can spell danger to sailors

definitions.text: that can spell danger to sailors

parts.note: light means flimsy, without weight or substance
a ship is a sea craft

explanation.surface: A ghostly vessel signals peril to seamen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spell danger' suggests a threat, but the moored vessel's beacon signals danger, warning sailors of a hazard such as a sandbank.
explanation.definitionFit: A moored vessel carrying a beacon warns mariners of shoals, signalling peril.

clue.text: Put off to discover the quarry has vanished

indicators.note: has vanished means a piece has gone, removed from the longer word

parts.note: to determine is to ascertain or find out
a mine is a pit dug for minerals, like a quarry

explanation.surface: A hunter is discouraged on finding the prey has disappeared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quarry' suggests hunted prey, but it is a pit, MINE, which 'has vanished' removes from DETERMINE.
explanation.definitionFit: To discourage or dissuade someone from acting is to put them off.

clue.text: The UK representative

parts.note: read as a diplomat or envoy, but meant as the helmeted female figure who personifies the nation on coins

explanation.surface: A diplomat speaking for the United Kingdom.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue suggests an ambassador; the representative is instead the symbolic figure with trident and shield standing for Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The helmeted woman with trident and shield is the national personification of Britain, so she symbolically represents the UK.

clue.text: Take a deep breath before start of the spectacle

indicators.note: before places the breath ahead of the next piece in the answer

parts.note: to sigh is to let out a long deep breath

indicators.note: the start of the word the is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone inhales deeply as the show begins.
explanation.definitionFit: A sight is something worth seeing, a spectacle, as in the sights of a city.

clue.text: A Belgian city's loyal people

explanation.surface: Residents of a Belgian town are faithful folk.
explanation.walkthrough: The Belgian city on the Meuse, written without its grave accent, plus 's for the possessive, gives the same letters as the plural of a feudal word for loyal subjects.
explanation.definitionFit: Belonging to a Belgian city in Wallonia; and loyal vassals or subjects bound to a feudal lord.

clue.text: Top man and creditor at odds

indicators.note: at odds means in disagreement or disorder, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: The boss and a lender are in dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at odds' rearranges the letters of 'creditor'.
explanation.definitionFit: A company director is one of the people at the top of a business, a boss.

clue.text: Getting gloomy over wrinkles in France

indicators.note: over, in a down clue, puts the first piece above the second

parts.note: grave means solemn and gloomy
lines are wrinkles on a face

explanation.surface: A Frenchman is becoming sombre and furrowed with age.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting' just links; the answer is a coastal town near Calais in northern France.
explanation.definitionFit: A port town in the Nord department, near Dunkirk, lies in France.

clue.text: Give voice about concern though not a lot

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the first word goes round the second

parts.note: to sing is to give voice to a tune
a matter is a concern or affair, as in a business matter

explanation.surface: Speak up about a worry, even if it is only a minor one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts SING round MATTER; 'though' just links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A smattering is a slight superficial knowledge or small amount, hardly much at all.

clue.text: Still spreading a vile tale

indicators.note: spreading means scattering about, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone keeps on circulating a nasty rumour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Still' looks like an adverb meaning continuing, but it is a verb meaning calm.
explanation.definitionFit: To still pain or fear is to calm or ease it, to relieve it.

clue.text: A fellow wants quiet after tea

indicators.note: after puts the quiet piece behind the tea piece

parts.note: cha is an old slang word for tea, from Chinese
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning quietly

explanation.surface: A man would like some peace and quiet once he has had his tea.
explanation.walkthrough: CHA is British slang for tea; P (piano) means quiet in musical notation.
explanation.definitionFit: Chap is informal British for a man or bloke.

clue.text: Take steps to bring this device into operation

definitions.text: Take steps to bring this device into operation

parts.words: Take steps to bring this device into operation
parts.note: taking steps reads as making arrangements, but literally walking is what makes a step-counting gadget work

explanation.surface: Make arrangements to get a machine running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take steps' means act, but here it means walk, which is what sets a step counter going.
explanation.definitionFit: A walker's gadget counts paces, so it only works when you walk.

clue.text: Being eccentric, I fish in this garment

parts.note: an eccentric is an off-centre wheel, a kind of cam in engineering
a sole is a flatfish

explanation.surface: Feeling odd, someone goes fishing wearing this piece of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentric' looks like an adjective about a person, but in engineering an eccentric is a cam, an off-centre wheel.
explanation.definitionFit: A light sleeveless women's undergarment or top is an item of clothing.

clue.text: Fish trodden underfoot

explanation.surface: A flatfish being stepped on.
explanation.definitionFit: A flatfish prized for eating; and the underside of a shoe or foot, the part that treads the ground.

clue.text: Drank too much — went beyond the limit

parts.note: over as a prefix means excessively, too much
lapped means drank with the tongue, like a cat

explanation.surface: A drinker overindulged and exceeded the legal limit.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a drunk driver; the pieces read in the opposite order to the clue's words.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that overlap extend past an edge onto one another, going beyond a boundary.

clue.text: The esplanade is full of cigarette ends for the time being

indicators.note: is full of means has something packed inside it

parts.note: a prom, short for promenade, is a seafront walkway

indicators.note: the ends of the word cigarette are its closing letters

explanation.surface: Seafront litter: the promenade is strewn with fag ends for now.
explanation.walkthrough: PROM is British for a seafront walkway; 'ends' takes the closing letters TE of 'cigarette'.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for temporarily, short for pro tempore, meaning for now.

clue.text: Relentlessly cut, see?

parts.note: to sever is to cut through
Ely is a cathedral city and bishop's see in Cambridgeshire

explanation.surface: Someone cut hard and without mercy, do you see?
explanation.walkthrough: A see is a bishop's diocese; ELY, a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire, England, is a crossword favourite for it.
explanation.definitionFit: Harshly or unsparingly done is done without letting up, without mercy.

clue.text: Mock food?

explanation.surface: Is this imitation grub?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mock food?' reads as fake or imitation food; both words are separate definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: To jeer at or ridicule; and, as slang, grub or something to eat.

clue.text: Microscopic alga, _ approximating to a dim blur

indicators.note: a blur is a smudged, jumbled image, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A tiny water plant looks like a faint smudge under the lens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'approximating' just links; 'blur' jumbles the letters of 'to a dim'.
explanation.definitionFit: A single-celled alga with a silica shell, visible only through a microscope.

clue.text: Pinching the feet

explanation.surface: Tight shoes squeezing someone's feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinching' looks like squeezing, but it is slang for stealing.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinching is slang for stealing, the crime of taking another's property.

clue.text: Some of the, old folks want a bird

indicators.note: some of means only part of these words is taken, the letters hidden inside them

explanation.surface: A few elderly people would like a pet bird.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'folks want'.
explanation.definitionFit: A large white waterbird with a long neck, a bird.

clue.text: Love some form of abstract painting

parts.note: love is nil in tennis, the round zero letter
some of something is a part of it

explanation.surface: Someone who loves a certain style of abstract art.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' as a verb disguises the tennis score of nil.
explanation.definitionFit: Optical art of the 1960s uses geometric patterns to trick the eye, an abstract style.

clue.text: Wooded area with no elders?

parts.note: a woodland that has only young trees, with no elder bushes or older members at all, a fresh planting

explanation.surface: A wood without any senior figures.
explanation.walkthrough: The name of a large Hampshire woodland and national park in southern England, read whimsically as a newly planted wood with no old trees.
explanation.definitionFit: A royal hunting forest in Hampshire, England, whose name humorously suggests young trees only.

clue.text: A secret society member frames one — so wrong

indicators.note: wrong means incorrect, put the wrong way, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A lodge member is framed for a crime, and it is unjust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'so' just links; 'wrong' rearranges the letters of 'frames one'.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of a fraternal order with private rituals, often called a secret society.

clue.text: Record always filled in by preservationists

indicators.note: filled in by means the first piece has another placed inside it

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, meaning always
the National Trust, a British heritage body, is abbreviated NT

explanation.surface: A heritage charity is forever filling in the archives.
explanation.walkthrough: The National Trust (NT) preserves historic houses and land in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: To log data is to put it down in a ledger, to record it.
